name: Pedro Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter on a timber apartment job on Harbour Road, six storeys built from CLT, which is cross-laminated timber, big wooden wall and floor panels made in a factory. I'm on site at 6:30, we do the toolbox talk, then the crane starts flying panels in and my gang screws them down and fixes the brackets. I love the moment a whole floor goes up in a day. What wears me out is the waiting, when a truck's late and eight of us stand around in hi-vis burning money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in that kind of work, and who do you work alongside?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did my trade certificate at 19 and spent five years on normal stick framing before I moved to this mass timber outfit. My gang is me, Tomasz, who's fifty-odd and has forgotten more than I know, and two younger lads still learning. I'm also the union delegate on site, so I end up in the site office arguing about breaks and harness checks more than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work? Money, home, that sort of thing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ines, who's a nurse on the cardiac ward, and we bought a small flat two years ago. The pay on this job is good, better than most carpentry, and we've got about ten months of costs put away. I use AI every day, honestly, for cut lists, checking fixing specs, and translating for the Portuguese lads on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the lunch hut: it's a good calculator with a big mouth. It saves me twenty minutes on a cut list and helps me read a German bracket spec, and that's about it. Nobody's screwing down a floor panel with a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life carries on pretty well. The work is steady, the timber builds are growing, and I'm good with the tools that exist. The thing that would still bug me is the stuff that was already broken: lads on day rates with no sick pay, and the pressure to rush the crane lifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push the union on the boring stuff, like getting the agency guys onto proper contracts by next spring. I'd keep using the AI apps for my own planning and show the younger lads how to check their cuts with it. Ines and I would keep putting about a fifth of our pay into savings like we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, to be honest. It's the world I already live in, and in that world I've got a good job and a good cushion. The only knot in my stomach is the same one I've always had, watching someone get hurt because a job was behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rushing the crane lifts. Can you tell me about a time that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March we were three days behind and the site manager wanted us flying panels in wind over the limit. Tomasz just sat down on a pallet and said he wasn't moving, and I backed him. We lost half a day and nobody got crushed, and that's the trade-off I'd make every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays small like this, is there anything you'd miss out on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit, because I actually like the tools and I hoped they'd take the paperwork off the foreman so he'd be out on the deck more. But I'm not going to cry about it. A good carpenter with a tape and a drill will be fine in this world.

say: I'd call AI a **good calculator** that helps with cut lists and specs but can't fix a panel.
I'd tell the lunch hut nothing **real changes** on a timber site in this world.
think: My **job and pay** stay solid, and timber building keeps growing.
The real problems stay the old ones: **day-rate workers** without sick pay and rushed crane lifts.
do: Push the union to get **agency workers** onto proper contracts by spring.
Keep using AI for **cut lists** and teach the younger carpenters to check their cuts.
Keep saving about **a fifth** of the household pay with my partner Ines.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, because this is the world he already does well in.
Still carries an old **knot of worry** about rushed lifts and injuries on site.
S0.quote: Nobody's screwing down a floor panel with a chatbot.
fieldNote: He uses AI daily and still sees it as a **small tool** in his own trade.
His worries in this picture are about **site safety** and agency workers, not technology.
The crane story shows he'll take a **cost to his pay** to back a workmate.

steps.text: Keep running the panel gang on the Harbour Road timber build
Push the site union to move agency carpenters onto contracts by spring
Teach the two apprentices to check cut lists with the AI app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get organised, because the office jobs are going first and the site jobs will change more slowly. At work I'd say we need to be in the room when the company brings in new software and robots, not told afterwards. Online I'd probably post too much about it, Ines tells me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good news, if I'm honest. The thinking parts of the job, like ordering, scheduling and reading drawings, get faster, and I'm already the guy who uses those tools. My hands are still on the drill for years, so I don't see my own pay dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask the company to put me on the team that tests the new planning software, because I'd rather shape it than be handed it. I'd sign up for the evening course on digital site setting-out, about two thousand to do over a winter, and we'd pay that from savings. Through the union I'd push for a training fund so the older carpenters aren't left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a bit of guilt mixed in. I'll probably come out of this better off, and I know people like the estimator and the site admin won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra, our site admin, does all the deliveries and permits and knows every truck driver by name. That's exactly the work software eats first. And Tomasz, who's brilliant with his hands but won't touch a tablet, so if the drawings all go digital he'll feel stupid, which he isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for someone like Sandra or Tomasz, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With Tomasz I'd just sit with him at lunch for a few weeks and show him the drawing app until it's boring. For Sandra I'd fight to get the company to retrain her as a site coordinator instead of letting her go. If they won't, that's a union fight I'd be glad to have.

say: I'd say workers need to be **in the room** when the company brings in software and robots.
I'd tell people the **office jobs** go first and site jobs change more slowly.
think: The **thinking parts** of his job get faster, and he's already good with those tools.
His **hands-on pay** looks safe for years, so this picture mostly helps him.
do: Volunteer for the team **testing** the company's new planning software.
Pay about **two thousand** from savings for a winter course in digital setting-out.
Push the union for a **training fund** for older carpenters.
feel: **Excited** about the new tools and where they could take him.
A little **guilty** that he gains while office colleagues lose out.
S1.quote: Sandra, our site admin, does all the deliveries and permits and knows every truck driver by name. That's exactly the work software eats first.
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **winner** here and is honest about feeling guilty for it.
His plans mix **personal upskilling** with collective action for weaker colleagues.
Notable that he names the **site admin**, not carpenters, as the first casualty.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the company's new planning and ordering software
Take the evening course in digital site setting-out this winter
Push the union for a paid training fund for older carpenters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is a political emergency, not a weather report. The people who own the robots shouldn't get to keep all the gains while millions of us get three years' notice. I'd be at every union meeting and probably every march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my trade has a sell-by date of about 2031, when I'm 32. The thinking side of the job, the ordering and planning, goes in 2028, so the foreman's role shrinks right away. I've got maybe five years of carpentry left and then I need to be something else, and I don't know what that is yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop the flat renovation we'd planned and keep every spare euro in savings, so we'd have closer to eighteen months. I'd try hard to get onto whatever crew runs and maintains the first site robots, because someone has to set them up and fix them. And I'd put real hours into the union's push for a wage guarantee or retraining fund paid for by the robot makers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, under the big talk. I've always felt like the one who's ahead of the tech, and in this picture being ahead only buys me a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be at every march. What would you actually be asking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A levy on companies that replace workers with robots, and that money going straight into retraining and a basic income for people like Tomasz. And a rule that a robot on a building site has a qualified human signing it off. I know that last one only buys time, but time is what we wouldn't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ines talk about at the kitchen table that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether her job is safer than mine, probably, because nursing has a lot of hands and heart in it. We'd talk about pushing kids back a few years, which hurts because we'd only just started talking about it. Ines would say we'll be fine, and I'd say we'll be fine, and neither of us would sleep.

say: I'd call this a **political emergency** and say robot owners can't keep all the gains.
I'd be at every **union meeting** and probably every march.
think: His carpentry work has a **sell-by date** of about 2031, when he turns 32.
The **planning side** goes in 2028, so the foreman role shrinks first.
He has about **five years** of carpentry left and no clear next job.
do: Cancel the **flat renovation** and stretch savings toward eighteen months.
Try to join the crew that **maintains site robots** when they arrive.
Spend real hours on a union push for a **robot levy** and retraining.
feel: Shaken that being **ahead of the tech** only buys a couple of years.
S2.quote: I've always felt like the one who's ahead of the tech, and in this picture being ahead only buys me a couple of years.
fieldNote: The three-year robot gap gives him **planning time**, not safety, and he knows it.
His public anger is about **who owns the gains**; privately he's frightened for himself.
Delaying **children** came up quickly, which shows how seriously he takes this.
Strong savings and his partner's nursing job keep him from **losing control**.

steps.text: Cancel the planned flat renovation and grow savings to 18 months
Apply to join the crew that sets up and fixes site robots
Campaign through the union for a robot levy funding retraining
Put off starting a family with Ines for a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same message as the fast one, just calmer: we've got five years, so let's use them to write the rules. I'd tell the lads on site not to panic but not to sleep on it either. Online I'd share every decent retraining scheme I find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2034 I'd be 35, and that's a different story from 32. I could get a real second skill in place, and the planning side of the job going in 2031 might even move me up into running robot crews. I'd say this one's a challenge I can actually plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time diploma in construction management, three years of evenings, so I'm qualified by the time the thinking AI lands. We'd keep saving the same fifth of our pay, and I'd go ahead with the flat renovation because the extra years make it worth it. With the union I'd help write a proper transition plan with the company, with dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. Five years of warning feels like knowing a big storm is coming and having time to fix the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why construction management, if AI does much of the planning by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, I thought about that while I was saying it. I think someone still has to be on site responsible for people and robots together, and be the one who signs things off. Even if the paperwork's done by software, someone has to stand on the deck and say no to a crane lift in the wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomasz in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz is about 55, so by 2034 he's around 63 and close to done anyway. In this version he can probably ride it out to retirement, which is one of the reasons I'm less scared here. It's the guys in their forties I'd lose sleep over.

say: I'd say we have **five years** and should use them to write the rules.
I'd tell colleagues not to panic but to **start preparing** now.
think: At **35** when robots arrive, he has time to build a second skill.
He might move up into **running robot crews** once the planning side changes.
do: Start a **three-year** part-time diploma in construction management.
Keep saving a **fifth** of household pay and go ahead with the flat renovation.
Help the union write a **transition plan** with the company, with dates.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, like seeing a storm coming with time to prepare.
S3.quote: Five years of warning feels like knowing a big storm is coming and having time to fix the roof.
fieldNote: Three extra years change his mood a lot; age **35 versus 32** matters to him.
He caught his own **contradiction** about management being automated and reasoned it through.
His worry shifts to **workers in their forties**, not himself or the near-retired.

steps.text: Enrol in a three-year evening diploma in construction management
Help the union write a dated transition plan with the builder
Go ahead with the flat renovation while still saving a fifth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly if we don't waste it. I'd be pushing for every apprentice starting now to get robot and software training built into the course. At work I'd probably be the annoying one with the timeline on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me personally ten years is plenty. By 2039 I'd be 40, with a management ticket and probably a few years running mixed crews. What bothers me is that ten years also lets everyone get lazy and think it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the setting-out course, then start the management diploma the year after, paced so I'm not wrecked. Ines and I would have our first kid like we've planned and keep saving steadily. In the union I'd push to rewrite the apprenticeship course with the local college so new carpenters learn to work with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but not switched off. I feel like I'd have a fair shot, and I'd be watching other people's backs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people might get lazy. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company, mostly, and the government. If it's ten years away the bosses will say it's not their problem yet, and then in 2035 they'll suddenly announce layoffs like it was a surprise. I've seen that with every safety rule we ever got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this slower picture that worries you more than the fast ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the apprentices. A kid starting at 17 now would be 30 when the robots come, which is exactly when you've finally got good. I'd hate to be the one training someone for a trade that disappears just as they're proud of it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if we don't waste it.
I'd push for every **apprentice** to get robot and software training built in.
think: By **2039** he'd be 40, qualified and likely running mixed crews.
His real fear is that bosses and government get **lazy** about a far-off deadline.
do: Finish the **setting-out course** first, then start the management diploma a year later.
Go ahead with a **first child** and keep saving steadily.
Work with the union and **local college** to rewrite the apprenticeship course.
feel: Still **watchful** for apprentices and older workers.
S4.quote: A kid starting at 17 now would be 30 when the robots come, which is exactly when you've finally got good.
fieldNote: Personally secure, but his mood stays **uneasy** because of the people around him.
His family plans go ahead in this picture, unlike the **fast one**.
He expects employers to treat a **ten-year warning** as nobody's problem.

steps.text: Finish the setting-out course, then start the management diploma
Have a first child with Ines as already planned
Work with the college to add robot training to apprenticeships

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The AGI by 2028 one, no question, because three years from AI to robots isn't enough for anyone to retrain, me included. What would help is a guarantee that if a robot takes my job, the company that owns it pays into a fund that keeps my wage going while I retrain. Paid retraining, not a pamphlet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets to decide. Everybody talks about AI like it's the weather, but somebody chooses to buy the robot and somebody chooses where the savings go. I'd want workers to have a seat at that table, on site and in government.

headlineQuote: Everybody talks about AI like it's the weather, but somebody chooses to buy the robot and somebody chooses where the savings go.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old carpenter** on a six-storey timber apartment build, and the site's union delegate.
He uses **AI daily** for cut lists and translation, and sees it as a tool he's ahead of.
In the mild pictures he's **calm**, focused on site safety and helping weaker colleagues.
AGI by 2028 frightens him because a **2031 robot date** leaves him at 32 with no next job.
With more warning he plans a **management diploma** and pushes the union for fair transition rules.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years between AI and robots is too short for anyone to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **robot-owner fund** that keeps his wage going while he retrains.
